# B326. Do the two PDF extractors agree about numbers?

Read-only diagnostic. No product code. No model calls. USD 0.
Ran 2026-09-24T13:11:10.183Z. officeparser wall 754600 ms. direct wall 1408 ms. pdfjs item dump 1109 ms.
Twenty PDFs: `scripts/diagnostic/delivery-check/b163/corpus/` via `catalog.json`. Same files as B163/B321. Not substituted.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 0A. FACTUAL CLAIMS
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

C1 BLOCKING. PARTLY. Line checked: `scripts/diagnostic/extractor-bakeoff/REPORT.md` L61, and `scripts/diagnostic/excerpt-recovery/REPORT.md` L11 and L100.
The bake-off report records arm A `25 th` and arm B `25th` on d17, and says the sentence is there. It does not say arm C dropped `th`.
`excerpt-recovery/REPORT.md` L11 records arm C live extract `the 25 anniversary` with `th` absent, and L100 repeats that arm C dropped `th` while arm B has `25th`.
This run's extracts confirm the three-way split: officeparser (arm A) `the 25 th anniversary`; direct (shipped arm C) `th` on the previous line and `the 25 anniversary` on the next. Arm C is what shipped (B321). Kill is FALSE-only, so the build proceeds.

C2 BLOCKING. TRUE. Line checked: `scripts/diagnostic/excerpt-recovery/REPORT.md` L100, and this run's d13 extracts.
excerpt-recovery L100: the d13 recovered window inserts the PDF's `1` and `2` footnote markers that sit inside the sentence.
This run, officeparser: `We earned revenue in 2024 of $180.6 billion 1 and net income of $58.5 billion, with return on tangible common equity (ROTCE) of 20% 2`.
This run, direct: the markers leave the sentence (`1` on the previous line, `2` on its own line before `equity`). The figures `$180.6`, `$58.5`, and `20%` are the same in both extracts. The Gate 7 quote in `extractor-swap/outputs/d13-gate7.json` L16 still carries `billion 1` and `20% 2` from the officeparser-era review.

C3 BLOCKING. TRUE. Assembly rule: `pageTextArmC` in `lib/extract-pdf-direct.mjs` L128-144.
`itemRecord` L119-126 stores only `str`, `x`, `y`. It does not store font size, height, or width.
`pageTextArmC` groups items by `Math.round(y)` into bands, sorts each band by `x`, and joins with a single space. Nothing in that function reads font size or a baseline other than the rounded y. An item whose y rounds to a different integer is sent to another line. An item whose y rounds to the same integer is treated as a peer of the body text, including a footnote marker or a superscript ordinal suffix.

C4 CHECK. TRUE. All twenty PDFs were on disk at `scripts/diagnostic/delivery-check/b163/corpus/` and both engines returned text.
Expected wall from B321: officeparser 755,629 ms; bake-off A 755,216 ms. This run: officeparser 754,600 ms, direct 1,408 ms. Matches.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 0B. DESIGN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

B0. Cursor design, written before the run.

A figure is a span that a reviewer could read as a quantity: currency amounts (`$180.6 billion`, `£659 million`, `CHF 2'136`), percentages (`20%`, `7.0%`), numbers with a magnitude word (`180.6 billion`), years and dates (`2024`, `31 March 2025`, `January 2`), bare numbers of two or more digits, and ordinals including the split form `25 th` that officeparser emits. Single-digit tokens are not figures. They would drown the inventory in list indices and table stubs, and they are not what a reader would treat as the number in a quote. If the data showed a 1-digit marker glued onto a figure, that shows up as DIGIT GAINED on the figure itself.

Inventories are built independently on each extract. Pairing is by collapsed left/right context tokens (last five tokens before, first five after), not by raw character offset. The two extracts wrap, insert page markers, and flatten tables in different orders, so the same figure does not sit at the same index. A Jaccard on the context tokens plus an exact key match plus a digit-gained bonus is the matcher. Unpaired figures are PRESENT/ABSENT.

Neither extract is truth. For every non-SAME pair, dump the raw pdfjs items in a +/- 6 item window around a digit hit, with x, y, width, fontSize, fontName. A smaller or raised digit in that window is the footnote/ordinal signature. The engine that glued an extra digit when that signature is present is the one that did not match the body glyph. Do not guess without the items.

A disagreement that also sits inside a recorded passage (`extractor-swap/outputs/` quotes and `delivery-check/b163/reviews/` excerpts) is a different severity from one that never left the extract.

This is an AMEND of naive offset pairing. Offset pairing would have labelled almost every wrapped paragraph a miss. The rest of B1-B6 is kept. The run used this design. There is no second parallel inventory.

B1 AGREE. The comparison is symmetric. S5 is allowed to say the old engine was worse, or that neither is reliable.
B2 AGREE. Raw pdfjs items are the tiebreaker. The diagnostic walks pdfjs itself. It does not change `extract-pdf-direct.mjs`.
B3 AGREE. Each S3 row records `inRecordedPassage` against the committed swap quotes and b163 review excerpts.
B4 AGREE, plus ordinals and the split form `25 th`. I did not widen to single-digit tokens. The motivating d13 footnote `1` / `2` are one character; they are recorded as an exhibit in S1 and S6 because they did not change the digits of `$180.6`. The inventory would have caught them if they had glued onto that figure (`$180.61` or `billion1`). They did not, on this regeneration.
B5 AGREE. Findings are reported and filed. No fix in this spec.
B6 AGREE. Assembly, excerpt logic, table detection, and production behaviour are untouched.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
S1. THE ANSWER
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The two extractions disagree about a number 1,148 times across the twenty documents (39 VALUE CHANGED, 458 DIGIT GAINED, 4 ORDINAL LOST, 647 PRESENT/ABSENT) against 6,761 SAME.
458 rows carry the digit-gained signature; 183 of those have a nearby smaller or raised digit in the raw pdfjs stream. The motivating d13 figure `$180.6` itself is identical in both extracts: officeparser leaves footnote `1` as a same-line token after `billion`, and direct moves that `1` onto the previous line. Neither glued it onto the dollars.
Seven of the 497 VALUE CHANGED and DIGIT GAINED rows matched a recorded reviewer passage. Inspecting those seven, they are table-adjacent pairings of different real numbers (`$180` against `$80`, `31 March 2025` against `31 March 2024`), not one quoted figure rewritten into another. The ordinal loss on d17 (`25 th` against `25`, with `th` on the previous line) is the mechanism's visible tip, and that sentence is a recorded Gate 7 quote.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
S4. ORDINALS
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

officeparser preserved 18 ordinals across the twenty (attached or split). direct preserved 11.
Paired class ORDINAL LOST: 4 (d08 x2, d17 x1, d19 x1). The other vanished ordinals on d08 sit in PRESENT/ABSENT because the matcher did not lock a partner.

Inventory of every ordinal span the two engines produced:

- d04 both: `1st` (effective 1st of the month).
- d08 officeparser: `28 th` (June 28 th meeting), `6 th` (6 th grade), `3 rd` (May 3 rd), `60 th` (60 th Anniversary). direct: zero. The suffix sits on the previous line in each case (`th` / `rd` then `June 28 meeting`, `6 grade`, `May 3 .`, `60 Anniversary issue`).
- d09 officeparser: `100th` (100th birthday) and `4 th` (4 th edition). direct: `100th` only. `th` sits two lines above `the new 4`.
- d11 both: `22nd`, `29th`, `1st`.
- d12 both: `22nd`, `1st`.
- d13 both: `16th`, `1st`, `2nd`.
- d17 officeparser: `25 th`. direct: none. `th` on the previous line, then `the 25 anniversary`. This is the C1 case.
- d19 officeparser: `24th` and `30 th`. direct: `24th` only. `th` on the previous line, then `its 30 anniversary`.

The attached form (`100th`, `22nd`, `1st`) survives both engines. The split form (`25 th`, `30 th`, `60 th`, `3 rd`, `4 th`, `6 th`, `28 th`) is what `pageTextArmC` loses, because the suffix is a separate item whose rounded y is not the body's. officeparser keeps those two items on one line with a space. That is the mechanism's visible tip. It does not change the digits. It strips the ordinal.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
S5. WHICH ENGINE IS RIGHT MORE OFTEN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

From B2, among the 497 VALUE CHANGED and DIGIT GAINED rows:

- superscript or raised digit seen in the dumped window: 190
- officeparser matches the body glyph (the other engine glued the extra digit): 114
- direct matches the body glyph (officeparser glued the extra digit): 76
- inconclusive (no superscript hint, or the windows did not isolate one marker): 307

Who has the longer digit string on DIGIT GAINED, without requiring a superscript hint: officeparser longer 232, direct longer 226. That split is a tie. It is also polluted by table mis-pairs (`$180` against `$80` is digit-gained by construction).

On the off-line-glyph subset this spec was written to measure, the old engine matched the body more often (114 against 76). The shipped engine is the one that more often absorbed the extra digit when a smaller or raised digit was in the window. That is not a finding that officeparser is generally more reliable. 6,761 figures are identical. 307 of 497 S3 rows are inconclusive, and most of those are flattened tables, which both engines still flatten (S6).

The ordinal count is the cleaner call, and it goes the same way. officeparser 18, direct 11. Every lost ordinal in this corpus is the shipped engine parking the suffix on the previous line. What shipped is worse at ordinals on these twenty. It is not worse at the dollars-and-cents of the d13 lead sentence: `$180.6`, `$58.5`, and `20%` are the same in both extracts.

If a later spec sizes a fix, the fix is for `pageTextArmC` treating a raised, smaller item as a peer of the body line. The ordinals are the exhibit. The footnote markers on d13 are the same exhibit with a one-character payload that this inventory, by B4, does not count as a figure.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
S6. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Documents outside these twenty. The corpus is the B163 set, not a sample of every PDF the product will see.
Non-Latin fonts. Neither engine configures `cMapUrl` / `cMapPacked` (B324). This run did not measure that.
Tables. Both engines flatten them. A large share of VALUE CHANGED and DIGIT GAINED on d01 and d13 is adjacent-cell pairing, not a glyph moving. The raw items in S3 show that. This spec does not add table detection (B6).
Single-digit footnote markers. B4 kept the two-or-more-digits floor. On d13 the markers `1` and `2` move between lines and do not glue onto `$180.6`. A glued `billion1` would have been DIGIT GAINED. Arm B of the bake-off had `$180.6 billion1`. Arm C, which shipped, does not, on this regeneration: it puts `1` on the previous line.
Pairing quality. Context-token pairing is better than raw offsets and still wrong in tables. Counts in S2 are therefore an upper bound on same-place disagreement.
Reviewer-visible harm from a rewritten figure inside a displayed excerpt. This run did not find one among the 497 S3 rows that both (a) changed the digits of the same figure and (b) sat inside a recorded passage as that figure. It did find the d17 ordinal loss in a recorded Gate 7 sentence. That sentence is how a reviewer would have seen `25` without `th`.
A fix. B5. Sizing the fix needs to know it is for off-line glyphs in `pageTextArmC`, not for a general number parser.

USD 0. No model calls.
